title: What do you do every day?
goal: Tell Sēf about your day: when you study, work, get home and play football.
tip: The present says what you do regularly. 'I' starts with a-, 'you' (to a man) with ti-, and questions need no 'do': adris (I study), tidris? (do you study?); arjaʿ (I get back), tirjaʿ? Add kill yōm (every day) or dōm (always): kill yōm alʿab kūra.
grammar: Present tense I: I (a-) and you to a man (ti-); habitual meaning
dialogue: What do you do every day?
In the morning I study, and in the afternoon I work.
And when do you get home?
أرجع بالمترو بعد الدوام، وأطبخ عشا
arjaʿ bil-mitro baʿd id-dawām, w aṭbakh ʿasha
I get back on the metro after work and cook dinner.
I do, but not every day.
أنا دوم ألعب يوم الجمعة، قريب منك. تعال!
ana dōm alʿab yōm il-jumʿa, garīb minnak. taʿāl!
I always play on Fridays, near you. Come along!
items: goes before the verb: dōm alʿab = I always play
you go back, you get back (to a man)
I go back, I get back
culture: Football is the most popular sport among Emiratis. In the hot months friends often play in the evening, after sunset, when it is cooler.

title: What are you studying, Maryam?
goal: At the office, with other colleagues around: ask Maryam when she leaves work, what she studies and where.
tip: To a woman, the 'you' verb adds -īn: tidris → tidrisīn, tiktib → tiktibīn, tiṭlaʿ → tiṭlaʿīn. So: Maryam, shu tidrisīn? (what are you studying?). 'Do you know?' is tadri? to a man and tadrīn? to a woman; tadrīn shu? means 'you know what?'
grammar: Present tense I: you to a woman: ti- + -īn (tidrisīn, tiṭlaʿīn)
dialogue: مريم، تطلعين من الدوام الساعة كم؟
Maryam, tiṭlaʿīn min id-dawām is-sāʿa cham?
Maryam, what time do you leave work?
الساعة ثلاث. وبعد الدوام أدرس كل يوم
is-sāʿa thalāth. w baʿd id-dawām adris kill yōm
At three. And after work I study every day.
A master's. And I'm writing a dissertation now!
Where do you write? At home?
No, in the library. Home's too busy!
تدرين شو؟ أنا بعد أدرس في مكتبة الجامعة
tadrīn shu? ana baʿad adris fi maktabat il-jāmʿa
You know what? I study in the university library too.
items: you go out, you leave (to a woman)
to a man: tiṭlaʿ (تطلع); tiṭlaʿīn min id-dawām = you leave work
to a man: tadri? (تدري؟); tadrīn shu? = you know what?

title: My brother studies medicine
goal: Hear Sēf talk about his sister's job and his brother's studies.
tip: 'He' starts with yi- and 'she' with ti-: yidris (he studies), tidris (she studies). So 'she works' and 'you (m.) work' sound the same, tishtaghil, and the context tells you which: ukhti tishtaghil wiyya Maryam. Negative: ma + verb, ma yitʿab (he doesn't get tired).
grammar: Present tense I: he (yi-) and she (ti-)
dialogue: تدري إن أختي تشتغل ويا مريم؟
tadri inn ukhti tishtaghil wiyya Maryam?
Did you know my sister works with Maryam?
la wallāh! w akhūk? yishtaghil baʿad?
No way! And your brother? Does he work too?
لا، يدرس طب، ودوم في المكتبة
la, yidris ṭibb, w dōm fi l-maktaba
No, he studies medicine, and he's always in the library.
ṭibb? yaʿni yidris lēl w nahār!
Medicine? So he studies day and night!
Yes, and he stays up late every night.
He does, but he really loves medicine.
items: do you know? did you know? (to a man)
to a woman: tadrīn? (تدرين؟); tadri inn … = did you know that …
day and night, all the time
ma yitʿab? = doesn't he get tired?

title: We go out on Fridays
goal: At Sēf's home, with Sēf there: tell Umm Sēf what you and Sēf do together on Fridays.
tip: 'We' starts with ni-: nilʿab (we play), niṭlaʿ (we go out), nis-har (we stay up). You can leave out niḥin, because ni- already means 'we': yōm il-jumʿa nilʿab kūra. Two verbs can follow each other with w: niṭlaʿ w nis-har.
grammar: Present tense I: we (ni-): nilʿab, niskin, niṭlaʿ
dialogue: inta w Sēf dōm wiyya baʿaẓ!
You and Sēf are always together!
هيه، ندرس في نفس الجامعة، ونسكن قريب
hē, nidris fi nafs il-jāmʿa, w niskin garīb
Yes, we study at the same university and live nearby.
And what do you get up to on Fridays?
نلعب كورة، ومرات نروح البحر ونسبح
nilʿab kūra, w marrāt nrūḥ il-baḥar w nisbaḥ
We play football, and sometimes we go to the beach and swim.
w marrāt niṭlaʿ w nis-har wiyya sh-shabāb
And sometimes we go out and stay up late with the guys.
w il-jāmʿa?! tadri inn il-imtiḥān garīb?
And university?! Do you know the exam is soon?
items: also very common: maʿa baʿaẓ (مع بعض)
what do you do? (to a group)
to one man: shu tsawwi?; to one woman: shu tsawwīn?
marrāt … w marrāt … = sometimes … and sometimes …
we stay up late, we spend the evening out

title: Do you all work here?
goal: At a karak stand, chat with two young men you have seen with Sēf, and get invited to football.
tip: For a group, 'you' and 'they' add -ūn: tilʿabūn (you all play), yilʿabūn (they play), tidrisūn (you all study). In longer verbs like tishtaghil, the short i before the last consonant drops: tishtaghlūn, yishtaghlūn (to a woman: tishtaghlīn). 'We' stays nishtaghil, with no ending.
grammar: Present tense I: you all (ti- … -ūn) and they (yi- … -ūn)
dialogue: هلا يا شباب! تدرسون ويا سيف؟
hala yā shabāb! tidrisūn wiyya Sēf?
Hi guys! Do you study with Sēf?
هلا فيك! لا، نشتغل في المطار
hala fīk! la, nishtaghil fi l-maṭār
Hi! No, we work at the airport.
ما شاء الله! تشتغلون كل يوم؟
mā shāʼ allāh! tishtaghlūn kill yōm?
Great! Do you work every day?
هيه، وأبوي وعمي يشتغلون هناك بعد
hē, w ubūy w ʿammi yishtaghlūn hnāk baʿad
Yes, and my dad and my uncle work there too.
w tilʿabūn kūra? Sēf dōm yilʿab!
And do you play football? Sēf plays all the time!
هيه، ربعنا يلعبون كل خميس. تبي تيي؟
hē, rabʿna yilʿabūn kill khamīs. tabi tiyi?
Yes, our mates play every Thursday. Want to come?
items: guys! (to a group of young men)
friendly, to young men you know or have just met
to one man: tishtaghil; to one woman: tishtaghlīn
to one man: tilʿab; to one woman: tilʿabīn
culture: Karak stands and cafeterias are where young men in Dubai often meet after work. Inviting a new acquaintance to a game straight away, as here, is ordinary friendliness.

title: Sēf doesn't study!
goal: At Sēf's home, with Sēf there: defend Sēf when his mother complains about his habits, and say what you don't do.
tip: Put ma before a present verb for 'don't': ma as-har (I don't stay up late), ma yidris (he doesn't study). The verb itself doesn't change. mub is for words that aren't verbs: mub zēn, mub kill yōm.
grammar: Present tense I: ma + present for 'don't, doesn't'
dialogue: سيف ما يدرس! دوم يلعب ويطلع
Sēf ma yidris! dōm yilʿab w yiṭlaʿ
Sēf doesn't study! He's always playing and going out.
لا يا أم سيف، يدرس، بس في الليل
la yā Umm Sēf, yidris, bas fi l-lēl
No, Umm Sēf, he does study, but at night.
والصبح ما يصحى! أصحيه، ويرجع ينام على طول
w iṣ-ṣubḥ ma yiṣḥa! aṣaḥḥīh, w yirjaʿ ynām ʿala ṭūl
And in the morning he doesn't wake up! I wake him, and he goes straight back to sleep.
w inta? tidris fi l-lēl baʿad?
And you? Do you study at night too?
لا، أنا ما أسهر. أدرس الصبح
la, ana ma as-har. adris iṣ-ṣubḥ
No, I don't stay up late. I study in the mornings.
ما شاء الله عليك! علمه شوي!
mā shāʼ allāh ʿalēk! ʿallmah shwayy!
Good for you! Teach him a bit!
items: good for you, well done (to a man)
to a woman: mā shāʼ allāh ʿalēch (ما شاء الله عليج)

title: Who does the shopping?
goal: Ask Sēf who goes to the supermarket in his family, and tease him about it.
tip: Hollow verbs keep a long vowel in the present: rāḥ → yrūḥ (he goes), shāf → yshūf (he sees), gāl → ygūl (he says), nām → ynām (he sleeps). No i- comes between the prefix and the stem: trūḥ, ashūf, anām. Endings work as before: tshūfīn, yrūḥūn.
grammar: Present tense II: hollow verbs with a long middle vowel (yrūḥ, yshūf, ygūl, ynām)
dialogue: Who goes to the supermarket in your house?
My dad, he goes every Saturday morning.
لا، ويا أمي. هي دوم تشوف الأسعار، وهو يدفع!
la, wiyya ummi. hiya dōm tshūf il-asʿār, w huwa yidfaʿ!
No, with my mum. She always checks the prices, and he pays!
And you? Don't you go with them?
لا، أنام! أبوي يقول: سيف ما يصحى!
la, anām! ubūy ygūl: Sēf ma yiṣḥa!
No, I sleep! My dad says, 'Sēf never wakes up!'
والله صح! تسهر كل ليلة، وانت كسلان
wallāh ṣaḥḥ! tis-har kill lēla, w inta kaslān
Honestly, he's right! You stay up every night, and you're lazy.
items: she sees, she checks; you see (to a man)

title: A walk after work
goal: At the office, with other colleagues around: ask Maryam what she does after work, and agree to start walking with Sēf.
tip: Verbs whose past ends in a vowel keep a vowel in the present: sawwa → ysawwi (he does), asawwi, nsawwi; misha → yimshi (he walks), amshi, timshi. Before -īn and -ūn the final i goes: tsawwi → tsawwīn, timshi → timshīn, yimshi → yimshūn.
grammar: Present tense II: verbs ending in a vowel (ysawwi, yimshi)
dialogue: Maryam, what do you do after work?
أمشي ساعة في الحديقة ويا أبوي
amshi sāʿa fi l-ḥadīga wiyya ubūy
I walk for an hour in the park with my dad.
Every day? Don't you get tired?
la, ʿādi. w inta? ma timshi?
No, it's fine. And you? Don't you walk?
لا، سيف يسوي رياضة، بس أنا كسلان!
la, Sēf ysawwi riyāẓa, bas ana kaslān!
No, Sēf does sport, but I'm lazy!
يلا، تمشي ويا سيف يوم الخميس؟
yalla, timshi wiyya Sēf yōm il-khamīs?
Come on, why not walk with Sēf on Thursday?
Why not! We'll walk early in the morning.
items: what do you do? what are you doing? (to a woman)
you walk (to a man); she walks
ysawwi riyāẓa = he does sport, he works out
culture: In a Dubai summer it is too hot to walk in the day, so people walk in the early morning, after sunset, or inside air-conditioned malls. In winter, parks and beach paths fill up in the evenings.

title: Moving into the flat
goal: Tell Sēf where to put things in your new flat while your phone rings.
tip: Doubled verbs end in a double consonant: ḥaṭṭ → yḥuṭṭ (he puts), aḥuṭṭ, nḥuṭṭ; radd → yrudd (he answers). Endings go straight on: tḥuṭṭīn, yḥuṭṭūn, nḥuṭṭha (we put it). The present is also used for 'shall I …?': wēn aḥuṭṭ il-karātīn?
grammar: Present tense II: doubled verbs (yḥuṭṭ, yrudd, ydigg)
dialogue: Where shall I put the boxes?
Put them in the room, by the window.
And the sofa? Shall we put it here?
هيه، قدام التلفزيون. أبوي دوم يحطها جي
hē, jiddām it-tilfizyōn. ubūy dōm yḥuṭṭha chī
Yes, in front of the TV. My dad always puts it like that.
هذي أمي. أرد عليها بعد ساعة
hādhi ummi. arudd ʿalēha baʿd sāʿa
It's my mum. I'll call her back in an hour.
لا يا ريّال، رد عليها الحين! لا تكون كسلان
la yā rayyāl, rudd ʿalēha l-ḥīn! la tkūn kaslān
No, man, answer her now! Don't be lazy.
items: we put it (a feminine thing) or them; shall we put it?
il-bāb ydigg = someone's at the door
arudd ʿalēh = I answer him, I call him back
to a woman: ruddi ʿalēha; answer him: rudd ʿalēh
only to friends of your age, never to an elder or in a meeting

title: I don't eat meat
goal: Order lunch with Sēf at the university cafeteria and say what you don't eat.
tip: kal (ate) and khadh (took) have a long ā in the present: ākil (I eat), tākil, yākil, nākil; ākhidh (I take, I'll have), tākhidh, yākhidh. To a woman: tāklīn, tākhdhīn; to a group: tāklūn, tākhdhūn. ākhidh also orders food: ākhidh simach.
grammar: Present tense II: kal and khadh: ākil (I eat), yākil, ākhidh (I take), yākhidh
dialogue: شو تاكل؟ أنا دوم آخذ عيش ولحم
shu tākil? ana dōm ākhidh ʿēsh w laḥam
What are you having? I always get rice and meat.
من زمان. آكل سمك ودياي بس
min zamān. ākil simach w diyāy bas
For ages. I only eat fish and chicken.
zēn, khudh simach. w tākhidh ʿaṣīr?
OK, get the fish. And will you have a juice?
لا، ماي بس. وآخذ سلطة بعد
la, māy bas. w ākhidh salaṭa baʿad
No, just water. And I'll get a salad too.
سمك وسلطة؟ أخوي يسوي رياضة، وياكل صحنين!
simach w salaṭa? akhūy ysawwi riyāẓa, w yākil ṣaḥnēn!
Fish and salad? My brother works out, and he eats two plates!
items: you eat; are you having? (to a man)
laḥam is red meat: chicken (diyāy) and fish are counted apart
you take; will you have? (to a man)

title: When are you coming?
goal: Take a call from Umm Sēf about lunch tomorrow, and tell her you love harees but don't know how to make it.
tip: 'Come': ayi (I), tiyi (you, to a man; she), yiyi (he), niyi (we); tiyīn to a woman, tiyūn to a group, yiyūn (they). 'It' or 'him' after a verb ending in a vowel is -īh: nsawwi → nsawwīh (we make it). After a consonant it's -ah: aḥibb → aḥibbah.
grammar: Present tense II: 'come' (ayi, tiyi, yiyi); object -īh after a vowel (nsawwīh)
dialogue: Salim, when are you coming tomorrow?
مشكورة! أيي الساعة وحدة إن شاء الله
mashkūra! ayi s-sāʿa waḥda in shāʼ allāh
Thank you! I'll come at one, God willing.
You're welcome. Is Sēf coming with you?
Yes, he's coming with me after work.
تحب الهريس؟ دوم نسويه يوم الجمعة
tḥibb il-harīs? dōm nsawwīh yōm il-jumʿa
Do you like harees? We always make it on Fridays.
أحبه وايد، بس ما أعرف أسويه
aḥibbah wāyid, bas ma aʿarf asawwīh
I love it, but I don't know how to make it.
ولا يهمك، أنا أسويه، وانت بس تاكل!
wala yhimmak, ana asawwīh, w inta bas tākil!
Don't worry, I'll make it. You just eat!
items: when are you coming? (to a man)
to a woman: mita tiyīn? (متى تيين؟)
she comes: tiyi (تيي); they come: yiyūn (ييون); you'll see written يي or يجي
we make it, we do it
I love it, I like him
I make it, I do it
ma aʿarf asawwīh = I don't know how to make it
culture: Harees, wheat cooked for hours with meat until smooth, is a traditional Emirati dish, served especially in Ramadan, at weddings and when honouring guests. Preparing and serving it is seen as a sign of hospitality and generosity.

title: The weekly shop
goal: Talk with Sēf at the supermarket about when you shop and how his dad shops.
tip: This lesson mixes the verb types: yilga (he finds) and yishtiri (he buys) end in a vowel like yimshi; yākhidh keeps its long ā; yṭāliʿ (he looks) is regular; yaʿṭi (he gives) ends in a vowel, so 'gives him' is yaʿṭīh. yākhidh wagt means 'it takes a long time'.
grammar: Present tense II recycled: yilga, yishtiri, yaʿṭi, yimshi, yṭāliʿ, yākhidh
dialogue: Do you come here every week?
هيه، كل سبت آخذ أغراض الأسبوع
hē, kill sabt ākhidh aghrāẓ il-usbūʿ
Yes, every Saturday I get the week's shopping.
And do you find everything here?
Yes, but the prices are a bit high.
أبوي يحب السوق. يمشي ويطالع ويشتري
ubūy yḥibb is-sūg. yimshi w yṭāliʿ w yishtiri
My dad loves the market. He walks around, looks and buys.
On his own? And does it take him long?
ساعتين! بس البياع دوم يعطيه سمك زين
sāʿtēn! bas il-bayyāʿ dōm yaʿṭīh simach zēn
Two hours! But the seller always gives him good fish.
items: aghrāẓ il-bēt = things for the house
you find (to a man); she finds
it takes a long time; he takes a long time
he takes his time (isn't in a hurry): yākhidh wagtah (ياخذ وقته)
he gives him: yaʿṭīh (يعطيه); give me: ʿaṭni
